evidence.label: Modularity of elliptic curves over imaginary quadratic fields

headline: Every elliptic curve over every imaginary quadratic field is claimed to match an automorphic form, place by place.
scope: The result covers every elliptic curve over every imaginary quadratic field, such as the field of numbers a + bi with a, b rational.
plain: An elliptic curve is a cubic equation whose solutions can be counted modulo each prime. Modularity says these counts are the coefficients of a highly symmetric function, an automorphic form. Over the rational numbers this was proved by 2001, completing work that gave Fermat's Last Theorem. The paper claims to prove it over every imaginary quadratic field, such as the numbers a + bi with a, b rational. It also claims the match holds at every prime, including the bad ones.
doesNot: This does not cover other fields, such as real quadratic fields or fields of higher degree.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: A. Wiles and R. Taylor–A. Wiles, who proved modularity for semistable elliptic curves over the rationals
scorecard.significanceWhy: Modularity over imaginary quadratic fields was known only for some curves or some fields, if this proof holds.

explanation:
Work with numbers of the form a + bi, where i² = −1 and a, b are fractions. Take the curve y² = x³ + x + i. To count its points modulo 5, note that 5 = (2 + i)(2 − i). Working modulo 2 + i turns i into 3, since 3² = 9 leaves −1 after dividing by 5. The curve becomes y² = x³ + x + 3 with remainders mod 5. It has 3 solutions with ordinary x and y, plus one point at infinity, so 4 points. The number 5 + 1 − 4 = 2 is the curve’s count at this prime.

An elliptic curve is an equation like this one, with no repeated roots on the right. Do the same count at every prime and you get an endless list of numbers. Modularity says one symmetric object produces that whole list. That object is an automorphic representation (a highly symmetric function built from the field, here acting by 2 × 2 matrices). The conjecture asks for even more. At the bad primes, where the curve breaks, the full local data must match too[1].

The field of numbers a + bi is one imaginary quadratic field. Others use √−2, √−3, and so on. Over the ordinary fractions, Wiles and Taylor–Wiles proved modularity for semistable curves in 1995. Breuil, Conrad, Diamond and Taylor finished every curve in 2001[3]. A key method lifts a match from a simpler “residual” version of the curve’s data, its pattern modulo one prime[4].

Imaginary quadratic fields resisted this method. The relevant data occur in more than one cohomology degree, a technical layer the method uses[5]. Potential modularity was proved: every curve becomes modular after enlarging the field[6]. But proving it over the original field is a further problem[7]. Caraiani and Newton proved modularity for some curves and fields. Their results include every curve over a field where a certain curve, X₀(15), has rank zero[8]. The paper claims to remove the remaining restrictions on the curve and the field[9]. It still relies on Caraiani and Newton’s lifting theorem as an essential input[9].

The paper claims the full statement[2]. For every imaginary quadratic field and every elliptic curve over it, a matching automorphic representation exists. The L-function of the curve (a function that packages all its point counts) equals the automorphic one, shifted by 1/2[10]. In the example, the count 2 at the prime 2 + i is one coefficient of a single automorphic object.

The obstacle is reaching a residual pattern that the known theorem accepts. The paper builds a chain of linked objects from one family of curves of higher genus[11]. Each link agrees with the next modulo a prime: first modulo p, then modulo 3, then modulo p again. Matches pass along the chain, from a curve at one end that is shown modular first, to the given curve. This echoes Wiles’s switch between the primes 3 and 5[13].

The claim stays inside its setting. It is about imaginary quadratic fields only. It does not cover real quadratic fields or larger fields.

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for this paper in the openai/math release. So no computer proof checker has checked it. The proof combines a new construction with deep published theorems. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Landmark only if the proof holds. No Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published. It covers imaginary quadratic fields only.

glossary.meaning: The solutions of a cubic equation like y² = x³ + ax + b with no repeated roots, plus one point at infinity.
The numbers a + b√−d with a, b fractions, for a fixed positive whole number d, such as a + bi.
Matched by an automorphic form, so the curve’s point counts are that form’s coefficients.
A highly symmetric object built from a number field whose numbers can match the counts of a curve.
A function that packages all the point counts of a curve, or all the numbers of an automorphic object.
The pattern of a curve’s symmetry data reduced modulo one prime.
Modularity that holds only after the field is enlarged.
